name: Hibiscus for hair

lead: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is a flowering tropical plant whose flowers and leaves appear in hair tonics, oils and masks. In traditional use the petals served as a hairpiece and, in China, as a black hair dye.

People use hibiscus preparations hoping for shinier, softer, fuller-looking hair. The appearance payoff is conditioning and colour rather than a proven change in hair density, and no clinical trial is documented here.

paras: Users apply hibiscus as oils, rinses, powdered petals or leaf pastes mixed into masks, usually on the scalp and lengths, and combine it with other herbal ingredients. Results reported by users are about slip, shine and softness after washing.
Topical plant products can cause skin irritation or allergy in some people. No published safety data on hibiscus hair products are cited here.

lead: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is a tropical ornamental plant whose flowers are used as a hair accessory, particularly as a hairpiece [1]. Traditionally in China the petals were turned into a black hair dye for women, and the flower has also been used for shoe polish and tea [1].

In modern hair care the plant is used as an extract in tonics, oils and masks for conditioning and shine. One study cited on Wikipedia showed a flower extract absorbing ultraviolet radiation, and the article says the plant may have potential in cosmetic skin care [1].
No clinical studies of hibiscus for hair growth or hair quality are cited in this article.

paras: The flower has been worn as a hairpiece, and in China its petals were made into a black hair dye [1]. It appears in cosmetic skin-care contexts because of its UV-absorbing flower extract [1].
The Wikipedia article reports that the flowers are edible and used in teas and salads [1]. Safety of topical hair products is not discussed in the cited sources.
